title: Ezekiel 29:1–16
context: Ezekiel 29–32 gathers the book’s oracles against Egypt, the last and longest set in the collection of words against the nations (chapters 25–32). Most of the oracles carry their own dates, counted from King Jehoiachin’s exile (1:2). Ezekiel 29:1–16 is dated to the tenth year, tenth month, twelfth day, a date often placed in early 587 BC, while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem; exact conversions to modern calendars vary slightly. The prophet reports the LORD’s word to him, addressed as son of man, and the LORD speaks against Pharaoh king of Egypt, picturing him as a great monster lying in the Nile who claims, "My river is my own, and I have made it for myself." The LORD will drag him out with hooks and leave him on the open field. Egypt has been a staff of reed to Israel, breaking when leaned on (compare 2 Kings 18:21 and Isaiah 36:6). The land will be desolate for forty years, after which the LORD will bring the Egyptians back to Pathros as a lowly kingdom that Israel will no longer trust. Ezekiel does not name the Pharaoh; many identify him with Hophra, whom Jeremiah names (Jeremiah 44:30), though that link is not certain. Both traditions read the unit as showing the LORD’s rule over the proudest of nations and his concern that his people trust him instead of Egypt.

verses.text: In the tenth year, in the tenth month, on the twelfth day of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet reports that the LORD’s word came to him on a specific date in the tenth year. Arminian readers see the care given to dating these oracles, which roots them in the real crisis of Jerusalem’s final siege.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the date as showing that God speaks into history. Both traditions note that the year is counted from Jehoiachin’s exile (1:2), and they hold the exact modern date loosely, often placing it in early 587 BC.

verses.text: “Son of man, set your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and prophesy against him and against all Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet, addressed as son of man, to set his face against Pharaoh and prophesy against all Egypt. Arminians see God’s authority reaching beyond Israel to the most powerful nations of the day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over all nations. Both traditions note that setting the face is Ezekiel’s repeated idiom for a firm word of judgment (compare 6:2 and 25:2).

verses.text: Speak and say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great monster that lies in the middle of his rivers, that has said, ‘My river is my own, and I have made it for myself.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he is against Pharaoh, the great monster in his rivers, who claims the Nile as his own creation. Arminian readers see pride that claims credit for what belongs to God, which is the root of Pharaoh’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the claim as a rival to God’s role as Creator. Both traditions read the monster as a figure perhaps drawing on the crocodile of the Nile, and they note that the boast is answered by the LORD’s sovereignty.

verses.text: I will put hooks in your jaws, and I will make the fish of your rivers stick to your scales. I will bring you up out of the middle of your rivers, with all the fish of your rivers which stick to your scales.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will put hooks in Pharaoh’s jaws and drag him out with the fish clinging to his scales. Arminians see a vivid picture of God’s power to humble the proud, using the image of a captured river creature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as showing that no power can resist God. Both traditions read the fish as Egypt’s people or allies, who share in Pharaoh’s fall, and they treat the image as poetic.

verses.text: I’ll cast you out into the wilderness, you and all the fish of your rivers. You’ll fall on the open field. You won’t be brought together or gathered. I have given you for food to the animals of the earth and to the birds of the sky.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will throw Pharaoh into the wilderness to lie unburied as food for animals and birds. Arminian readers see the shame of being denied burial, which was a terrible fate in the ancient world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reversal of Pharaoh’s greatness. Both traditions note that Egyptian kings took great care over burial, which makes this picture of an unburied death especially striking.

verses.text: “ ‘ “All the inhabitants of Egypt will know that I am the LORD, because they have been a staff of reed to the house of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says all Egypt will know that he is the LORD, because they were a staff of reed to Israel. Arminians see judgment that reveals God’s identity, and they see Egypt held responsible for failing those who trusted it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the refrain as showing God’s purpose to make himself known. Both traditions compare 2 Kings 18:21 and Isaiah 36:6, where Egypt is also called a reed that pierces those who lean on it.

verses.text: When they took hold of you by your hand, you broke and tore all their shoulders. When they leaned on you, you broke and paralyzed all of their thighs.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that when Israel leaned on Egypt, it broke and injured them. Arminian readers see the danger of trusting human powers instead of God, which left Israel wounded rather than helped.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a warning against misplaced trust. Both traditions read it as addressing Judah’s hope in Egypt during the Babylonian crisis, and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: “ ‘Therefore the Lord GOD says: “Behold, I will bring a sword on you, and will cut off man and animal from you.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he will bring a sword on Egypt and cut off people and animals. Arminians see God’s judgment falling on Egypt in response to its pride and its harm to others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign control over war. Both traditions read the sword as the invading army, and they note that how God uses such powers is discussed at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: The land of Egypt will be a desolation and a waste. Then they will know that I am the LORD. “ ‘ “Because he has said, ‘The river is mine, and I have made it,’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Egypt will be a desolation, and they will know he is the LORD, because Pharaoh claimed the river as his own. Arminian readers see the link between pride and judgment, which the verse makes explicit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s glory displayed in humbling the proud. Both traditions hold this as shared ground: God opposes those who claim his glory for themselves.

verses.text: therefore, behold, I am against you and against your rivers. I will make the land of Egypt an utter waste and desolation, from the tower of Seveneh even to the border of Ethiopia.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will make Egypt a waste from the tower of Seveneh to the border of Ethiopia. Arminians see the scope of the judgment, reaching from one end of Egypt to the other.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the phrase as covering the whole land. Both traditions note that Seveneh is usually identified with Syene, modern Aswan, at Egypt’s southern border, though they hold the geography of the phrase with some care.

verses.text: No foot of man will pass through it, nor will any animal foot pass through it. It won’t be inhabited for forty years.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says no foot of person or animal will pass through Egypt, and it will be uninhabited for forty years. Arminian readers see a period of judgment that is real but limited, echoing Israel’s forty years in the wilderness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God setting the length of the judgment. Both traditions note that the forty years may be a round number for a generation, and they avoid forcing it onto a precise historical period.

verses.text: I will make the land of Egypt a desolation in the middle of the countries that are desolate. Her cities among the cities that are laid waste will be a desolation forty years. I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countries.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Egypt will be desolate among desolate countries for forty years, and its people scattered. Arminians see Egypt sharing the fate of other nations, including Judah, whose people were also scattered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice applied to all nations. Both traditions read the scattering as a judgment like the exile of Judah, showing that God’s standards apply beyond Israel.

verses.text: “ ‘For the Lord GOD says: “At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the peoples where they were scattered.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says that after forty years he will gather the Egyptians from where they were scattered. Arminian readers see God’s mercy even toward a judged nation, which shows that his purposes include restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign control over both judgment and restoration. Both traditions find it striking that Egypt also receives a promise of return, and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: I will reverse the captivity of Egypt, and will cause them to return into the land of Pathros, into the land of their birth. There they will be a lowly kingdom.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will restore Egypt’s fortunes and bring them back to Pathros, where they will be a lowly kingdom. Arminians see restoration that comes with humility, since Egypt will never again be the power it was.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God limiting Egypt’s future greatness. Both traditions note that Pathros refers to southern or Upper Egypt, which some see as the land of Egypt’s origins.

verses.text: It will be the lowest of the kingdoms. It won’t lift itself up above the nations any more. I will diminish them so that they will no longer rule over the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Egypt will be the lowest of kingdoms and will never again rule over nations. Arminian readers see the humbling of pride as the purpose of the judgment, so that Egypt will no longer exalt itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over the rise and fall of nations. Both traditions read the verse as a reversal of Pharaoh’s boast in verse 3, and they hold it as shared ground.

verses.text: It will no longer be the confidence of the house of Israel, bringing iniquity to memory, when they turn to look after them. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Egypt will no longer be Israel’s confidence, reminding them of their sin in turning to it, and they will know he is the Lord GOD. Arminians see God removing a false object of trust so that his people will rely on him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s care for his people’s faithfulness. Both traditions read the verse as showing that Egypt’s judgment serves Israel’s good by ending a temptation to trust human power.
